Header: Dasyses rugosella , Euzopherodes vapidella and Erechthias minuscula

Prevention: Clean the storage facility and avoid storing damaged tubers.
Use clean planting stock that does not have moth eggs or caterpillars on it.
Try not to pierce or damage the yams during harvest, as this can provide an easy access point for the yam moths.
If using a temperature-controlled storage facility, storing the tubers between 12°C and 20°C will delay the development of the moths and help control damage.
Be careful not to store below 12°C as this will cause chilling damage to the tubers.
Monitoring: Monitor regularly for symptoms on tubers during harvest and storage as yam moths are post-harvest pests of yam tubers:
Euzopherodes vapidella lay eggs in wounds on the surfaces of the tubers soon after harvest.
The larvae bore into the tubers during harvest and storage, leaving tunnels.
This causes the tubers to deteriorate, decreasing the value of the crop.
Look for black frass (faecal matter) woven together by silk threads left by larvae and pupa cases that are left behind after the adult emerges.
The tineid moths ( Dasyses rugosella and
Erechthias minuscula ) are a secondary pest that attack the tubers once the pyralid moths have already caused damage and the yams have lost moisture.
The tineid larvae eat the inside of the tuber leaving only the skin.
Direct Control: Do not store tubers that show signs of damage with undamaged tubers.
Sort the tubers prior to storage and keep the damaged tubers separate.
To prevent hatching and emergence of the adult moth, apply by lightly dusting pepper powder (sweet pepper
Capsicum annum and chili pepper) on cuts or other visible damage on the yam tuber surface.
The powder can persist for 14 days and continue to provide control during that time.
